record.paper_title: Padua points and “fake” nodes for polynomial approximation: old, new and open problems
record.original_question: For bivariate Lagrange interpolation at Padua points in the square [-1,1]^2, can one prove or otherwise fully explain the observed fact that the Lebesgue function attains its maxima at the four corner points even though those corner points are not Padua interpolation nodes?

evidence.quote: The Lebesgue function has its maxima in the corners, where there are no Padua points.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega = [-1,1]^2$ and for each integer $n \geq 1$ let $\mathrm{Pad}_n \subset \Omega$ denote the set of Padua points of degree $n$, that is, the set of self-intersections and boundary endpoints of the generating curve
$$\gamma_n(t) = (\cos((n+1)t),\, \cos(nt)), \qquad t \in [0,\pi],$$
which forms a unisolvent set of cardinality $\binom{n+2}{2}$ for the space $\Pi_n^2$ of bivariate polynomials of total degree at most $n$. For $\xi \in \mathrm{Pad}_n$, let $\ell_\xi \in \Pi_n^2$ denote the corresponding Lagrange fundamental polynomial, characterized by $\ell_\xi(\eta) = \delta_{\xi,\eta}$ for every $\eta \in \mathrm{Pad}_n$. The Lebesgue function associated with $\mathrm{Pad}_n$ is
$$\lambda_n(x,y) = \sum_{\xi \in \mathrm{Pad}_n} |\ell_\xi(x,y)|, \qquad (x,y) \in \Omega,$$
and the Lebesgue constant is $\Lambda_n = \max_{(x,y)\in\Omega} \lambda_n(x,y)$.

Note that, depending on the chosen family, only two of the four corners $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$ of $\Omega$ belong to $\mathrm{Pad}_n$ (one pair of opposite corners). Numerical evidence indicates that for every $n$ the function $\lambda_n$ attains its maximum value $\Lambda_n$ at the four corners $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$ of $\Omega$, including at the two corners that are not Padua interpolation nodes.

Prove (or otherwise rigorously explain) that for all $n \geq 1$,
$$\Lambda_n = \lambda_n(1,1) = \lambda_n(1,-1) = \lambda_n(-1,1) = \lambda_n(-1,-1),$$
and that this maximum is not attained at any interior point of $\Omega$.
artifact.status_search_result: The phenomenon that the Lebesgue function of the Padua points attains its maxima at the four corners of the square—including the two corners that are not interpolation nodes—is widely reported as a numerically observed fact in the literature on Padua points, but no proof or full theoretical explanation appears to have been published. The asymptotic O(log² n) growth of the Lebesgue constant has been rigorously established, but the precise localization of the maxima at all four corners remains stated as an open question.

status_evidence.title: Bivariate Lagrange interpolation at the Padua points: the generating curve approach
status_evidence.snippet: Padua points have Lebesgue constant of order O((log n)^2), the minimal order of growth for bivariate polynomial interpolation.
status_evidence.claim: The optimal log-squared growth of the Lebesgue constant is established, but localization of its maxima at corners is not proved.

status_evidence.title: Padua points - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The Padua points are the first known example of a unisolvent point set with minimal growth of their Lebesgue constant, proven to be O(log^2 n).
status_evidence.claim: Standard references record the optimal Lebesgue constant growth without addressing the exact location of the maximum.
